passage: Coach's note, Lalit, under-12 kho-kho. Gopika joined in June and for weeks stood alone at the edge while the girls stretched in a circle. Today, after she tagged out two runners in the final, the team lifted her onto their shoulders. Afterwards the captain tied the team's orange ribbon on her wrist. Gopika touched it all through the bus ride home and kept laughing at nothing. She told me, "Now I'm really in the team." I will keep an eye out that the quieter girls feel part of it too.

qa.q: What did the captain tie on Gopika's wrist?
qa.a: The team's orange ribbon.

qa.q: What does Gopika touching the ribbon all the way home suggest?
qa.a: She felt safe and happy at last to be accepted, and the ribbon was proof she belonged. 🧡

qa.q: Why is Lalit's plan to watch the quieter girls wise?
qa.a: Belonging matters deeply at this age, so making sure no one stays at the edge keeps the whole team secure.

qa.q: What was the team's experience of lifting Gopika?
qa.a: They were celebrating her tags and, maybe without planning it, showing her she was fully one of them.

grounding: It shows, in a coach's note, a girl's deep security and joy once her team accepts her.

passage:
Diary, Friday.
Today Alka said, "Yogesh, you're coming to the science club picnic, na? We kept a spot for you." They'd even written my name on the list with a star. For months I've eaten lunch alone watching their table. Today I sat in the middle. Everyone laughed at my bad joke about the frog. Nobody asked why I talk funny. I wasn't nervous once. I think this is what my cousins mean when they say "our gang." Walking home, I felt like I could carry a whole sack of cement. 😊

qa.q: What did the group put next to Yogesh's name on the list?
qa.a: A star, written with Yogesh's name on the list.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel sitting in the middle of the table?
qa.a: Relaxed and secure, not nervous at all, because the group had made room for Yogesh and laughed along.

qa.q: How could Yogesh make this belonging last and pass it on?
qa.a: Keep showing up to the club, and later save a spot for someone else who eats alone.

qa.q: What might Alka have noticed before inviting Yogesh?
qa.a: Perhaps that Yogesh had been eating alone for months, so keeping a spot was Alka's way of welcoming Yogesh in.

grounding: It shows a child's strong sense of security and worth after a peer group finally includes them.

passage: Every autumn the boys of the para built their own small pandal behind the pond, and Anirban had always watched from his grandmother's veranda. This year Hemant, who ran the group, shouted up, "Anirban! Can you paint? Come!" He ran down so fast he left his slippers behind. They gave him the lion's mane to paint. By evening his hands were yellow, and the other boys were calling him "Lion-babu." On the way home he kept looking back at the lit pandal. That night he told his grandmother, "Next year, they said I can do the eyes."

qa.q: Which part did the boys give Anirban to paint?
qa.a: The lion's mane.

qa.q: What does Anirban running down without his slippers show?
qa.a: He had longed to be part of the group for years and was thrilled to be invited in.

qa.q: How could Hemant help other watching children feel welcome too?
qa.a: Keep calling out to children on the edge and give each one a real job, the way he did with Anirban.

qa.q: How might Anirban's grandmother see the change in him?
qa.a: She may be happy to see him glowing after years of watching from the veranda.

grounding: It shows a small-town boy's joy and security when a peer group takes him in and gives him a nickname.

passage: On Kofi's first week at a new school in London, he ate lunch alone. On Thursday, a girl named Elif stopped by his table. 'You're the one who hums while you draw. We're a band. We need a drummer. Can you tap?' Kofi tapped a rhythm on the table. Elif grinned. That afternoon he sat on the floor of the music room with four other kids, all tapping pencils. When they finished a song, they all cheered, and someone slapped his back. Walking home, Kofi felt lighter than he had in weeks.

qa.q: What did Elif's band need?
qa.a: They needed a drummer.

qa.q: Why did Kofi feel lighter walking home?
qa.a: Being accepted into the band gave him a sense of belonging after a lonely first week.

qa.q: What could Kofi do to strengthen this new sense of belonging?
qa.a: He could keep turning up for practice and get to know each band member better.

qa.q: How might Elif see inviting Kofi?
qa.a: She likely saw it as finding the drummer they needed, and may be glad he fitted in so well. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a child finding emotional security and validation in being accepted by a peer group, in England.

passage: In her first month at the girls' hostel, Swati cried quietly under her blanket most nights. Then one Friday, Mahima from the next bed whispered, 'We share snacks at ten. Come.' Six girls sat in a circle on the floor with a torch, passing namkeen and gossiping. They asked Swati about her village and laughed at her story about the goat who ate her homework. Mahima tied a friendship thread on her wrist. That night Swati fell asleep smiling, the thread still on her wrist, feeling for the first time that she was one of them.

qa.q: What did Mahima tie on Swati's wrist?
qa.a: She tied a friendship thread.

qa.q: Why did Swati fall asleep smiling that night?
qa.a: She felt accepted and secure for the first time since arriving, because the girls welcomed her.

qa.q: How could the hostel help other new students feel this way?
qa.a: Staff or older students could make sure newcomers are invited to groups early, instead of leaving it to chance.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel about inviting Swati?
qa.a: She likely feels good about helping a lonely new girl join them. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child finding security and validation through acceptance into a peer group at a hostel.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Raghav's older brother. Raghav, eleven, has been trying to get into the colony football team for a year. Last week the captain finally said, "You're in." Raghav came home glowing. He wore the blue jersey to dinner and then to bed. Now he talks about "we" all the time: "We won," "We practise at six." He used to be quiet at family gatherings, but yesterday he told everyone about the match. I don't know exactly what it means to him, but he walks differently now.

qa.q: What colour is the team jersey?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What does Raghav wearing the jersey to bed suggest?
qa.a: He feels proud and secure, deeply happy to belong to the team at last.

qa.q: How could Raghav's family support his new sense of belonging?
qa.a: Show interest in his matches and cheer for the team, while keeping home a place he's valued too.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see the change in Raghav?
qa.a: He notices Raghav is more confident and talkative, though he can only guess what it means inside.

grounding: Shows a child's joy and security at being accepted into a team, seen by an older brother.

passage: First week at the new school: Asif, ten, ate lunch alone under the stairs. Second week: Joseph, a boy from his class, asked, "You play carrom?" Asif joined their lunch group. He mostly listened. Fourth week: someone mentioned "the jalebi incident", and everyone looked at Asif and laughed, because it had been his joke. Asif laughed so hard his eyes watered. That night he told his mother, "I have a group now." He slept better than he had in months.

qa.q: What did Joseph ask Asif?
qa.a: "You play carrom?"

qa.q: How did Asif feel when everyone laughed at his old joke?
qa.a: He felt accepted and deeply happy, because the group now shared jokes that included him.

qa.q: What helped Asif move from eating alone to belonging?
qa.a: Joseph's simple invitation and Asif staying, listening and joining in over weeks.

qa.q: What might Joseph feel seeing Asif laugh with the group?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, glad that his invitation worked out.

grounding: Shows a child moving from loneliness to secure belonging in a peer group over a month.

passage: "Beta, I was eleven when we moved to the town, and no one talked to me. Then I saw girls playing kabaddi behind the school. Their captain was Rukmini, tall, with a loud laugh. I stood at the edge for three days. On the fourth, she shouted, 'Hey, new girl! We need one more!' I ran in, fell in the dust, and they all laughed, but not at me. After the game, Rukmini put her arm around my shoulders. That night I, your Farida Nani, cried from happiness. I still remember the smell of that dust."

qa.q: How many days did young Farida stand at the edge?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: Why did young Farida cry that night?
qa.a: She felt so happy and relieved to finally be accepted by the girls.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Farida?
qa.a: Rukmini calling her in to play on the fourth day.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have seen the new girl at the edge?
qa.a: She probably noticed her waiting and wanted to include her, maybe remembering being new herself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child she found deep security in being accepted by a kabaddi team.

passage: Chetan had joined the Chembur cricket team only two weeks ago. On Sunday the match was stopped by rain after one over. The boys crowded under a tin shed, wet and cold. Chetan stood at the edge, not sure where to go. Then Vidya, the captain, shouted, "Oi, new guy, get in here!" and pulled him into the middle. They started the team chant, and someone thumped his back. Chetan didn't know all the words yet, but he shouted anyway. For the first time since moving, he felt warm, even though his shirt was soaked. "Same time next week?" Vidya asked. "Definitely," Chetan said.

qa.q: How long had Chetan been on the team?
qa.a: Only two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he shouted the chant?
qa.a: He felt accepted and happy, warm inside for the first time since moving.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped Chetan feel he belonged?
qa.a: Vidya called him into the middle of the group, drawing him into the chant.

qa.q: How might the team captain see Chetan by the end?
qa.a: Vidya likely sees him as part of the team now, happy he joined the chant.

grounding: A new boy under a shed in the rain feels he truly belongs when the cricket team pulls him into their chant.

passage: In the Powai colony, the boys with cycles rode round the park every evening. Saurabh had watched for months from his balcony. When he finally got a second-hand cycle, he rode slowly near the gate. Francis, the oldest, circled back. "You're the one on the fourth floor, right? Come." By the third round they were calling him "Speedy," because he'd almost crashed into a bench. Saurabh laughed louder than anyone. At home he couldn't stop talking about it. "They gave me a name, Mummy. A real one." He went to bed smiling.

qa.q: What did the boys start calling Saurabh?
qa.a: "Speedy."

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel about getting a nickname?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and accepted, as though he was truly part of the group.

qa.q: What could Saurabh's mother say to support him?
qa.a: She could share his happiness and ask about the new friends, while encouraging him to keep his other friendships too.

qa.q: How might Francis see the new boy?
qa.a: Francis likely sees Saurabh as a friendly addition and enjoys welcoming him.

grounding: A boy finds deep happiness in being accepted and nicknamed by a colony cycle group.

passage:
"Harish Bhaiya! Guess what!"
"You found a kitten?"
"No! The dance group asked me to join. For the annual day!"
"The same group that didn't pick you last year?"
"Yes! Kritika said they need me for the front row. And they saved me a seat at lunch." Yamini spun round. "They all have matching hair clips, and they said they'll get me one."
"You're really happy, huh?"
"I don't feel like an outsider anymore." She stopped. "Do you think they'll still want me if I mess up the steps?"
Harish smiled. "They picked you. Practise, and ask them for help."

qa.q: What did the group say they would get Yamini?
qa.a: A matching hair clip.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she said, "I don't feel like an outsider anymore"?
qa.a: She felt happy and secure, with a deep sense of belonging, though also a little worried about messing up.

qa.q: What did Harish advise Yamini to do?
qa.a: To practise and ask the group for help.

qa.q: How might Harish see his sister's excitement?
qa.a: Harish seems pleased for her, remembering she wasn't picked last year.

grounding: A girl tells her brother how accepted she feels after being invited into a dance group.

passage:
I remember the day I got my team jersey. I was eleven, and I'd been trying to get into the school football team for a whole year.

After practice, Aparna, the captain, threw a jersey at me. "Number 7. You're in."

I held it and couldn't speak. Then the others clapped, and someone put an arm round my shoulders.

That night I wore it to bed. For the first time at school, I didn't feel like the odd one out. I felt like part of something.

I'm Hafsa, and I still have that jersey in my cupboard.

qa.q: What number was on Hafsa's jersey?
qa.a: Number 7.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when the team clapped?
qa.a: Hafsa felt overwhelmed with joy and accepted, like part of something.

qa.q: How could a coach help new players feel they belong?
qa.a: A coach could welcome them warmly, give them a team role, and encourage the others to include them.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel giving Hafsa the jersey?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt pleased and proud to welcome a hardworking player.

grounding: A child remembers the security and joy of being accepted into the school football team.

passage:
Swimming camp note, summer.

Farida joined the camp late, in the second week, and spent the first days sitting alone at the edge of the pool during breaks.

On Thursday, the group of girls she swims with invited her to their relay team. They practised the handover together and cheered when she finished her lap.

Since then, Farida walks in smiling and sits with them at break. Her mother told me she talks about the "relay girls" all evening.

I've kept the relay team together for the final. — Manjula

qa.q: When did Farida join the camp?
qa.a: She joined the camp late, in the second week.

qa.q: How has Farida felt since joining the relay team?
qa.a: Farida feels happy and secure, walking in smiling and talking about the "relay girls" at home.

qa.q: How did Manjula support Farida's belonging?
qa.a: Manjula kept the relay team together for the final.

qa.q: How might the relay girls feel about Farida?
qa.a: They seem to welcome and value her, cheering her lap.

grounding: A swimming coach notes a child finding security and happiness in being accepted into a relay team.

passage:
Ganesh Chaturthi, day 3

Today Kavitha Didi asked if I wanted to join the building dhol group! Only the big kids play in it, and I've been watching them from the balcony for two years.

She gave me the smallest dhol and showed me the beat. I got it wrong at first. Nobody laughed. They just played slower till I caught up.

When we played for the aarti, everyone in the building clapped. Kavitha Didi winked at me.

I didn't want to go home. I kept thinking, I'm one of them now.

Pooja

qa.q: What instrument did Kavitha Didi give Pooja?
qa.a: She gave Pooja the smallest dhol.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when the building clapped?
qa.a: Pooja felt thrilled and proud, like belonging to the group.

qa.q: How did the group help Pooja feel accepted?
qa.a: They didn't laugh at mistakes and played slower until Pooja caught up.

qa.q: How might Kavitha Didi feel about including Pooja?
qa.a: Kavitha Didi likely felt glad and warm, winking to show approval.

grounding: During Ganesh Chaturthi, a child writes about feeling accepted into the building's dhol group.

passage: Dolma's family had moved to the hill town of Ravangla only a month before Losar. At school she ate lunch alone on the steps. The week before the new year, Irawati's group was cutting paper lanterns in the corner of the classroom. Irawati looked up. "Dolma, you know how to make the eight-point ones, right? Show us?" Dolma folded, snipped and opened a perfect star. The others crowded round. "You're in our group for the fair," Irawati declared. That evening Dolma ran all the way up the steep lane and told her Ama three times, "I'm in Irawati's group." She slept with the paper star under her pillow.

qa.q: What were Irawati's group cutting in the corner of the classroom?
qa.a: They were cutting paper lanterns.

qa.q: Why did Dolma tell her Ama three times, "I'm in Irawati's group"?
qa.a: She felt joyful and secure at last after weeks of eating alone, and the acceptance meant a great deal to her. 🤍

qa.q: How could a teacher help new students like Dolma feel included sooner?
qa.a: The teacher could set up small group tasks early and invite new students to share a skill, as Irawati did.

qa.q: What might Irawati gain by inviting Dolma?
qa.a: Irawati's group gains a skilled lantern maker, and Irawati may feel good about welcoming someone new.

grounding: Shows a new child finding deep security and happiness in being accepted by a classmates' group before a festival.
